solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What mollusc inhabits ocean's lower regions?

parts.note: the ocean is the sea, so ocean's gives sea's
the lower regions is a euphemism for hell, the underworld

explanation.surface: A quiz question asking what sort of creature lives in the deepest parts of the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: The '?' flags a riddle: the question 'what does a mollusc inhabit?' is answered by splitting the word, so its home is the ocean's underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: A mollusc such as a whelk or cockle lives within its protective casing, the shell found on beaches.

clue.text: Rue eroticism that's deviant and only superficially attractive

indicators.note: something deviant departs from the normal order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A disapproving remark about kinky erotica being regrettable and merely skin-deep in its appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Meretricious describes something showy and alluring on the surface but lacking real value or substance.

clue.text: Unscramble lyric after a month

indicators.note: the lyric comes after the month in the answer, so the order is month then poem

parts.note: Dec is the short form of December, a month
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: A puzzle fan sets to unjumbling a song text once a month has gone by.
explanation.definitionFit: To decode a coded message is to unscramble it back into plain, readable language.

clue.text: The Queen always up for respect

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the pieces are read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword abbreviation for the Queen
ever means always, as in for ever

explanation.surface: A loyal subject declares that the monarch is perpetually deserving of esteem.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere someone is to hold them in deep respect or awe, a verb of veneration.

clue.text: Formerly working with civil engineer

parts.note: a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Someone recalls that they used to be employed alongside a civil engineer.
explanation.definitionFit: Once means at some time in the past, previously, just as formerly does.

clue.text: Grim at all times in southeast

indicators.note: the phrase for always is placed inside the compass abbreviation

parts.note: SE is the compass abbreviation for southeast
ever means at all times, always

explanation.surface: A gloomy complaint that the south-east of England is perpetually dreary.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe and grim both describe something stern, harsh or forbidding in manner or outlook.

clue.text: Fur belonging to myself after earl, oddly

indicators.note: the word for belonging to myself comes after the letters from earl
oddly means take the odd-numbered letters, first and third, of the word earl

parts.note: something belonging to myself is mine

explanation.surface: A peer claims the fur trim on his robe is his own, rather strangely.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine is the white winter coat of the stoat, the fur traditionally trimming peers' ceremonial robes.

clue.text: Short word some feel bally son omitted to send back

indicators.note: sending back means the chosen letters are read in reverse order
some of the words means only part of their run of letters is used

explanation.surface: A curt instruction to return some feeling, the son having forgotten to post it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks ELBALLYSONOM out of the run of letters, and 'to send back' turns it round. 'bally' is old British slang meaning bloody or blasted.
explanation.definitionFit: A monosyllable is a word of just one syllable, so it is necessarily a short word.

clue.text: Man, say, in Paisley

indicators.note: in means the letters sit inside the word Paisley, unchanged

explanation.surface: A man, perhaps, living in the Scottish town of Paisley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person but is the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea; Paisley is a town near Glasgow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an island, so Man is an example of an isle, flagged by say.

clue.text: Shrub with red or white flowers — unusually red alone

definitions.text: Shrub with red or white flowers

indicators.note: unusually means in an unusual arrangement, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A gardener notes a bush whose blooms are red or white, oddly with only red showing.
explanation.definitionFit: Oleander is a Mediterranean evergreen bush bearing showy pink, crimson or white blossoms.

clue.text: Brief respite with time for papa to recover

indicators.note: time standing for papa means one letter replaces the other

parts.note: a reprieve is a brief respite or temporary relief
Papa is P in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A short break, with time spent with dad, to get one's strength back.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrieve something is to get it back or regain possession of it, as in recover.

clue.text: Contend with immoral behaviour, shunning clubs

indicators.note: shunning means avoiding, so the clubs letter is left out

parts.note: vice is immoral or wicked behaviour
C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit

explanation.surface: Someone battles with depravity while steering clear of nightclubs.
explanation.definitionFit: To vie is to compete or strive for something against rivals, so it means contend.

clue.text: Indifferent emergency appeal gains nought

parts.note: SOS is the international distress signal, an emergency appeal for help
nought, zero, looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A charity's urgent appeal for funds raises nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so means neither good nor bad, mediocre, which is the sense of indifferent as in an indifferent performance.

clue.text: Bony eel takes cooking

indicators.note: cooking means the letters are being worked over and changed into something new

parts.note: as printed these words give three Es and one L; the anagram needs one E to be an L, a slip in the clue

explanation.surface: A thin eel is put on to cook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooking' is the anagram signal, but the printed 'eel takes' has three Es and one L where the answer needs two of each: a setter's slip the blog passed over.
explanation.definitionFit: Skeletal describes someone so thin that their bones show, which is what bony means.

clue.text: Co-operating group assembling Brexit, Labour or Conservative leaders

indicators.note: the leaders of the words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A political alliance brings together supporters of Brexit, Labour or the Conservatives.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is an alliance of parties or nations acting together for a common purpose.

clue.text: Still on the sea bed around California and Maine

indicators.note: the bed goes around the two state abbreviations

parts.note: taken as written
ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine

explanation.surface: A sea bed somewhere off the coasts of California and Maine lies motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: A becalmed sailing ship is stuck motionless at sea for lack of wind.

clue.text: Barley regularly ends in new ale and beer for him?

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of Barley, at regular intervals
the ends of the following words are their final letters

explanation.surface: Barley and the final touches of fresh ale and beer are the domain of one tradesman.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer: barley and ale and beer are the stuff of the man who brews them, so 'him?' points to the person the clue is about.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewer makes beer and ale from barley, so he is the person the clue's ingredients are for.

clue.text: Quit after Conservative split

indicators.note: quit is placed after the Conservative letter, so the order is the letter then the word

parts.note: to quit is to leave

explanation.surface: A politician resigns after a Conservative party split.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleave is to split or cut apart, as with an axe or cleaver.

clue.text: Paraffin oil's odd treatment for sore knee

indicators.note: an odd treatment handles the letters strangely, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An unusual remedy for an aching knee involves rubbing it with paraffin.
explanation.definitionFit: Kerosene is the American and technical name for paraffin, a fuel oil used in lamps and heaters.

clue.text: Former partner with morning paper

parts.note: an ex is a former partner or spouse
AM, ante meridiem, means morning

explanation.surface: An ex comes round with the morning newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: An exam paper is a written test, so a paper here is an examination.

clue.text: A mostly concrete neighbourhood

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word but not all, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: concrete means real, actual rather than abstract

explanation.surface: A district largely built of concrete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concrete' looks like building material but means real, here losing its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An area is a district or part of a town, the same as a neighbourhood.

clue.text: Fool in hospital left ecstasy — bother

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
an ass is a fool
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: An idiot in hospital has quit taking the drug ecstasy, causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' only joins: the fool sits after the hospital letter, since a single letter cannot be cut open.
explanation.definitionFit: Hassle is trouble, annoyance or inconvenience, the same as bother as a noun.

clue.text: Coarse east European taking Victor for British

indicators.note: taking means the east European takes on the new letter
Victor for British means one letter replaces the other

parts.note: a Bulgar is a Bulgarian, an east European
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A rude east European receives a medal for Britain, a Victoria Cross perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Vulgar and coarse both describe crude, unrefined or indecent behaviour or language.
